title: Impact-driven piezoelectric energy harvester using a pendulum structure for low-frequency vibration
venue: Journal of Intelligent Materials Systems and Structures

sections.heading: Impact-driven piezoelectric energy harvester using a pendulum structure for low-frequency vibration
sections.text: Guifen Fan1,2, Yanjiong Wang $^ { 1 , 2 } _ { \mathbb { D } , }$ , Feng Tian1,2, Mengmeng Hao1,2, Yue Wen1,2, Yanzhe $\mathbf { \ x } _ { \mathbf { u } } ^ { 1 , 2 }$ , FangFang Zeng1,2 and Wenzhong Lu1,2

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text: This study investigates a pendulum ball impact-excited piezoelectric energy harvester (PEH) for low frequency vibration through finite element analysis and experimental verification. This structure can harvest the vibration energy of infrasonic level, which provides a new idea for the energy harvest of low frequency. Experimental results show that for a pendulum ball impact-excited PEH with a $2 . 5 ~ \mathsf { m m }$ horizontal displacement excitation at $_ { 2 \mathsf { H z } }$ , namely the sinusoidal excitation acceleration of $0 . 0 4 ~ g ,$ the collision frequency between the pendulum and the cantilevers reaches $| 0 \ H \mathbf { z } ,$ , and the open-circuit peak voltage of two piezoelectric cantilevers in the collision is 30.1 and 27.1 V respectively. Under the parallel connection of two piezoelectric cantilevers, the open-circuit peak voltage is $1 5 . 8 \lor$ and a maximum output power of $1 0 . 5 3 ~ \mu \mathsf { W }$ can be achieved across a $1 3 0 ~ \mathsf { k } \Omega$ external load resistance. Compared with a single pendulum ball structure, a bi-pendulum ball structure can interact with two cantilever beams in one collision, thereby improving the efficiency of energy collection and reducing the optimal load resistance. A maximum output power of $4 3 \ \mu \mathsf { W }$ can be achieved across a $4 7 \ \mathsf { kOmega }$ external load resistance and $_ { 2 \mathsf { H z } }$ rotational vibration excitation.

sections.heading: Keywords
sections.text: Finite element analysis, low-frequency vibration, pendulum, piezoelectric energy harvester

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
As a promising approach that can replace the use of batteries to power wireless sensor networks, vibration energy harvesting has garnered an extensive growing attention. In recent years, substantial research has revealed that extracting electric energy from environmental vibration energy is feasible (Beeby et al., 2006). Although the output electric energy is in the microwatt to milliwatt level, it is enough to supply low-power electronic devices to enable energy-autonomous systems. Three major types of vibration-to-electric energy conversion mechanisms are described as electrostatic (Zhu et al., 2010), electromagnetic (Sari et al., 2008), and piezoelectric (Saadon and Sidek, 2011). Among these three alternatives for vibration energy harvesting, the piezoelectric energy harvester (PEH) has attracted the most attention due to its high energy density, no reliance on initial voltage, simple structure, and good compatibility with micro electric–mechanical systems.

The piezoelectric cantilever beam is the most common structure used in PEHs, which operates in a bending mode and provides low resonant frequencies and large strain in the piezoelectric patches to generate electrical power (Ajitsaria et al., 2007; Cottone et al., 2012; Erturk and Inman, 2007, 2009; Wang, 2013). To improve the efficiency of energy conversion, researchers have conducted many studies on piezoelectric materials (Anton and Sodano, 2007), the shape optimization of cantilever beams (Hu et al., 2006), electromechanical conversion mode (Kim et al., 2013), and energy harvesting interface circuits (Liang et al., 2011). However, Once the excitation frequency slightly shifts from the resonance frequency of piezoeletric cantilever beams, power generation is drastically reduced, resulting in a narrow operating frequency bandwidth. To overcome this drawback, Zhu et al. (2010) summarized and compared many different strategies to adjust or tune the resonant frequency; these strategies included vibrating beam arrays, multimodal vibration, and active or adaptive frequency-tuning methods. Fundamentally, in many practical cases, ambient vibration, such as ocean undulation or human motion, occurs at infrasonic frequency ranges, which deviate far from the resonant frequency of piezoeletric cantilever beams. For piezoelectric cantilever beams, achieving a large energy output to harvest the low frequency is difficult.

For capturing ambient vibration energy, the bistable configuration and the frequency up-conversion technique have been proposed. Harne and Wang (2013) presented an analytical framework for bistable electromechanical dynamics and summarized the wide variety of bistable energy harvesters, including magnetic repulsion harvester, magnetic attraction, and buckled beam harvesters. However, the main challenge for these nonlinear devices is how to obtain large output power in a large bandwidth. The frequency up-conversion technique is a method that can transform low-frequency ambient vibration into the high-frequency resonance of a piezoelectric cantilever beam through mechanical impact. As such, the energy conversion efficiency of the low-frequency vibration is improved. An impact-driven and frequency up-conversion technique for energy harvesting was first proposed by Umeda et al. (1996). In such technique, a steel ball impacted a piezoelectric membrane and transformed mechanical energy to electric energy. Gu et al. (2011) presented an impact-driven, coupled vibration energy harvester composed of a low-frequency driving beam and a high-frequency generating beam based on frequency up-conversion technology. When the excitation acceleration is $0 . 4 \ \mathrm { g }$ and the frequency is $8 . 2 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ , the collision frequency is $5 7 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and the maximum output power is $4 2 9 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ . A similar structure of PEH was theoretically and experimentally demonstrated by Halim et al. (2014); When the excitation acceleration is $6 ~ \mathrm { m / s } ^ { 2 }$ , the structure produces output power of $2 3 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ at the lowest and $3 7 8 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ at the highest in the frequency range of $7 ~ \mathrm { H z } \mathrm { - } 1 4 . 5 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . Wei et al. (2013) presented and demonstrated an impactdriven PEH, which uses the frequency up-conversion strategy and converts low-frequency human body motion into high-frequency vibration required by the piezoelectric bimorphs. An open-circuit voltage of $2 . 4 7 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ and a maximum average power of $5 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ can be achieved with a $2 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ external load resistance and a $5 ~ \mathrm { k m ~ h } ^ { - 1 }$ walking speed.

There has been much research on pendulum-excited energy harvesting. Xu et al. (2015, 2017) suspended a single pendulum on the free end of the cantilever beam, which can realize the multi-direction energy collection of the single cantilever beam. The theoretical analysis of modes and experimental results show that by applying the excitation acceleration of $0 . 0 0 8 \ \mathrm { g }$ in the $x$ , y, and $z$ directions, the peak open circuit voltages generated by the structure are 3.01, 3.01, and $3 . 2 7 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , respectively.

Ramezanpour et al. (2016) designed a piezoelectric energy harvester for extracting vibrational energy from a rotating shaft. A magnet is placed at the free end of a cantilever beam and placed near a magnet attached to the shaft. When the rotation angular velocity is $1 0 . 4 7 ~ \mathrm { r a d / s }$ , the structure can produce a peak output voltage of about 5 V. Wu et al. (2018) proposed a simple piezoelectric spring structure based on a common binder clip. Under the excitation acceleration of $0 . 2 6 \ \mathrm { g } .$ , the maximum output power of $1 3 . 2 9 \ \mathrm { m W }$ can be generated. Although these single-pendulum structures have many advantages, such as multi-directional energy capture or better output performance, they cannot capture energy at ultra-low frequencies of a few Hertz. In order to capture the vibrational energy of the subsonic level, a pendulum structure with the frequency up-conversion technique is proposed. Cui et al. (2015) designed a single-pendulum piezoelectric energy absorber, which works at the infrasound level. The structure consists of two cantilevered beams and a swinging ball. If the length of the fixed end is not added, the space occupied by the structure is $1 0 0 \times 1 0 \times 1 3 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ . Through experimental research, it is concluded that after the excitation acceleration of $0 . 1 \ \mathrm { g }$ is applied, the maximum output power of the device is about $3 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ . Because the output power is too low, it is necessary to optimize it to meet the needs of electronic devices.

In this study, a pendulum ball impact-excited PEH based on a frequency up-conversion strategy is proposed. Since frequency up-conversion can increase extracted power, this system has potential usefulness. Basically, the double-impact structure means that the frequency of impacts is greater than the driving frequency (a first up-conversion), and the still-higher resonant frequency of the energy harvesting beams provides a second frequency up-conversion. This has the potential to offer improved performance as compared with more conventional impact-based energy harvesters. Because we need to know the relation of the energy harvested by this structure with time, and the finite element analysis is very suitable for the simulation of time dynamics, so we will use the finite element analysis method here. The finite element analysis (FEA), physical production, and performance testing of the harvester are discussed below.

sections.heading: Finite element simulation analysis of a pendulum ball impact-excited PEH
sections.text:
A schematic of a pendulum ball impact-excited PEH is shown in Figure 1. It includes a low-frequency pendulum and two high-frequency piezoelectric cantilever beams. Two piezoelectric cantilever beams are fixed on either side of the mass block above. The mass block is empty inside, and the pendulum can swing around the rotating shaft. The pendulum is hung in the middle of two piezoelectric cantilevers and parallel to them. When the pendulum is driven by external excitation, the ball impacts the piezoelectric cantilever beams, and the piezoelectric cantilever beams vibrate with its resonant frequency after they separate. Such action results in the generation of a peak voltage. ![](images/cac3330de70a4a003d6461e72d69e6a1b6af13dc40b7b0fe94b54b842e771fff.jpg) Figure 1. ANSYS is used to build a numerical model with the coupling of piezoelectricity, circuit, and vibration for the energy harvester connected directly with a load resistor. A 20-node hexahedral coupled-field element (SOLID226) is used for the piezoelectric material, whereas a 20-node linear structural element (SOLID186) is used for the metal material. A circuit element (CIRCU94) is used to model load resistance. The flowing current, the across voltage, and the dissipated power of the load resistance can be calculated using the frequency response. The load resistor is connected to the top and bottom electrodes of the piezoelectric plate. The meshed FEA model of the single pendulum ball impact-excited PEH was established by ANSYS. The material properties and structural parameters of the pendulum in the harvester are listed in Table 2. When a $z$ -directional vibration is applied on the fixed part of the PEH, the pendulum can swing and impact the two cantilevers. Through periodical mechanical impact between the pendulum ball and two cantilevers, the energy harvester converts the ambient vibration or impact with low frequency to vibration of the cantilevers with high frequency. The Rayleigh damping form is introduced into the transient analysis. The coefficients for the mass and stiffness matrices are $\alpha$ and $\beta$ , respectively. In the model, $\alpha$ is 0, whereas $\beta ~ = ~ 0 . 0 0 0 5$ . The amplitude of the sinusoidal displacement excitation applied to the fixture is $2 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ , and the initial frequency is $2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , that is, the applied sinusoidal excitation acceleration is $0 . 0 4 ~ \mathrm { g }$ . The open-circuit voltages generated by the left and right piezoelectric patches are simulated, as shown Figure 2. According to the result of FEA, when the pendulum is driven by external excitation, the ball impacts the piezoelectric cantilever beams with the generated peak voltage, and the piezoelectric cantilever beam vibrates with its resonant frequency after they separate. Furthermore, the output terminals of two piezoelectric cantilevers are connected in parallel to increase the output current. The opencircuit output voltage when the same sinusoidal displacement excitation is applied is shown in Figure 3. ![](images/1395236d0c3acc8e2b6662f2ce7d90fa94004af3a16fe1af4f88e9a0448a098c.jpg) Figure 2. (a) Open-circuit output voltage of the left and right piezoelectric cantilever beams under the impact of the pendulum ball (b) output voltage waveform in $| - 1 . 5 \ s$ . ![](images/3b093a3aa74bb9047c4be5bb629f98a280d9b71df816ecb0cd88d054d5f1b7dc.jpg) Figure 3. Open-circuit output voltage of two piezoelectric cantilever beams connected in parallel under the remote displacement excitation. As shown in the Figures 2 and 3, after the excitation is applied to the device, the device reaches a stable state at about $0 . 0 8 3 \mathrm { ~ s ~ }$ . That is, the external low-frequency vibration can be transformed into a high-frequency collision of the cantilever beams. When the external vibration frequency is $2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , the collision frequency between the pendulum ball and the two cantilever beams reaches $1 2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . The peak value of the output voltage produced by the collision of each beam reaches $3 6 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ . In parallel mode, only one piezoelectric cantilever beam can be collided at a time, causing another cantilever beam to act automatically as its load. Then, the peak value of the output voltage decreases to $1 5 \ \mathrm { V }$ when collision occurs. The effect of the distance $\Delta _ { 0 }$ between the ball and the cantilever beam on the output performance is simulated and analyzed to improve the deformation caused by collision. Under the same excitation conditions, the open-circuit voltage curves at different distance $\Delta _ { 0 }$ are shown in Figure 4. The output voltage has a maximum value at a distance $\Delta _ { 0 }$ of $3 \mathrm { \ m m }$ . With the further increase in the distance $\Delta _ { 0 }$ , the collision between the pendulum and the cantilever beam begins to weaken until no collision occurs. A proper distance $\Delta _ { 0 }$ between the ball and the cantilever beams can increase the impact velocity.

sections.heading: Experiment and discussion
sections.text:
A pendulum ball impact-excited PEH is fabricated to verify the output characteristics of the PEH, and its performance testing experimental setup is exhibited in Figure 5. The energy harvester’s dimensions and material properties are listed in Tables 1 and 2. The electromagnetic vibrator (Jiangsu Sinocera Piezotronics, HEAS-2) is driven by a matching power amplifier and a signal generator (Jiangsu Sinocera Piezotronics, YE-1311). An accelerometer (Jiangsu Sinocera Piezotronics, CA-YD-107) is attached onto the electromagnetic vibrator near the energy harvester to measure the acceleration. The displacement amplitude and frequency of vibration can be measured using a vibration measuring instrument (Jiangsu Sinocera Piezotronics, SA-CJ01A). The output voltage is measured using an oscilloscope (American Agilent, DSO-X2022A). By adjusting the signal generator to produce lowfrequency signals, the fixed platform connected with the exciter can create a sinusoidal reciprocating motion. The output terminals of the two piezoelectric cantilevers are connected with the load resistance, and the voltage and output power on the load are measured using an oscilloscope.

![](images/bacace64efcd5aafb640b4d72f996ff09651548cb3dca839aa6dcb2bb129f17a.jpg)  
Figure 4. Open-circuit voltage curves at different distance $\Delta _ { 0 }$

![](images/6078625af2b54a232d5e360d3b8414b6b820f5734e04a2e5f5fd0dcd67e3b775.jpg)  
Figure 5. Experimental setup.

Figure 6 presents the measured open-circuit output voltage waveform of the energy harvester under an ambient excitation of $2 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ displacement and $2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ frequency. As shown in Figure 6(a) and (b), the time interval between adjacent voltage peaks is roughly $0 . 1 \ s$ according to the measured output voltage waveform; hence, the collision frequency between the ball and the piezoelectric cantilever beam is approximately $1 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . When the ball collides with the left or right piezoelectric cantilever, the peak output voltage is 30.1 and $2 7 . 1 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , respectively. When it is connected in parallel, the peak voltage drops to $1 5 . 8 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , as shown in Figure 6(c). The vibration test results are consistent with the finite element simulation results.

The output voltage of the PEH is proportional to the external electrical load, as shown in Figure 7. Under the parallel connection of two piezoelectric cantilever beams, a maximum output power of $1 0 . 5 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ can be achieved with a $1 3 0 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ external load resistance.

![](images/2a498bbec006791c52672dc5742216a9f7e56a0a87fc855d902c2cf1d1a2d560.jpg)  
Figure 6. Measured open-circuit output voltage waveform versus time under an excitation of $2 . 5 ~ \mathsf { m m }$ displacement and $2 H z$ frequency (The excitation acceleration is $\boldsymbol { 0 . 0 4 \ g } )$ : (a) left piezoelectric cantilever, (b) right piezoelectric cantilever, and (c) two piezoelectric cantilever in parallel.

![](images/9e1b9c5d8a607eada8bb7cf6dd75f8e5b35c7ee89e85afc6a2e6648fad6b881b.jpg)  
Figure 7. Output voltage and output power of the singlependulum structure PEH with various external resistors.

Considering the application background, such as collecting vibration energy from wave fluctuation or human motion, higher output voltage and power are required. For this vibration, a bi-pendulum ball impact-excited PEH is proposed. The 3D model and photographic views of the bi-pendulum ball impactexcited PEH prototype are shown in Figure 8(a) and (b). Here, a rotational excitation velocity is used. The rotational acceleration applied to the fixture is $0 . 0 5 8 \ \mathrm { g }$ , and the initial frequency is $2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . The open-circuit voltage of four piezoelectric cantilevers connected in parallel is obtained via FEA and experimental test, as presented in Figure 9(a) and (b). The results show that the collision frequency between the pendulum ball and the piezoelectric cantilever beams is approximately $1 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . The peak values of the open-circuit output voltage for the simulated and experimental results are approximately 12 and $1 0 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , respectively.

The impedance spectra of a single-pendulum- and bipendulum-structure PEH are measured using an impedance analyzer (Agilent 4294A, Keysight Technologies,

USA), as shown in Figure 10. The internal impedance of the PEH can be effectively reduced by using the bipendulum structure, which can produce a high output power under low load resistance.

The output voltage and average output power of the PEH with various external resistors obtained through experiment are shown in Figure 11. A maximum output power of $4 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ can be achieved across a $4 7 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ external load resistance and $2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ rotational vibration excitation. Compared with that of the single-pendulum structure, the maximum output power of the bipendulum structure is considerably enhanced.

The comparison of output performance of four kinds of energy capture structures are shown in Table 3. The simulation data of traditional cantilever beam is attached. Although the traditional cantilever beam structure has better output performance, the vibration frequency is too high, so it cannot meet our application requirements. The simple pendulum structure designed by Cui et al. (2015) is similar to this paper. However, the output power density of the structure is too low at the vibration frequency of $5 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ . In this paper, the output performance of the single pendulum structure is greatly improved at lower vibration frequency. When the applied excitation acceleration is $0 . 0 4 ~ \mathrm { g }$ and the vibration frequency is $2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , the maximum output power of the structure is $1 0 . 5 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ . The maximum output power density is about six times higher than the structure designed by Cui et al. Under the rotation excitation acceleration of $0 . 0 5 8 \ \mathrm { g } $ , the maximum output power of the bi-pendulum structure is $4 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ . This is in line with the expected experimental results. The experimental and simulated open circuit voltage data agree well, which proves the feasibility of the structure.

Although the maximum output power of the bipendulum ball structure is four times that of the single pendulum ball structure, its volume is twice that of the single pendulum ball structure, so the output power density basically remains unchanged. However, the bipendulum pendulum structure has other advantages over the single pendulum structure. First, for some applications, relatively high output power is required.

considering the practical application scenario, there are various forms of vibration around us. For example, in the common environment of ocean fluctuations or human activities, the common forms of vibration are fluctuations, swinging back and forth, or rotation, etc. In this environment, compared with the single pendulum-ball structure which can only oscillate horizontally, the bi-pendulum ball structure can better satisfy the actual vibration environment. Third, the matching impedance of the bi-pendulum ball structure is smaller, and it is easier to design the matching circuit for energy collection. Finally, compared with the use of two separate single pendulum structures, the bipendulum ball structure make the device more compact. This can improve the utilization of space. Of course, this is more in line with the experimental objectives I expected to achieve.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, this study demonstrates the design, simulation, fabrication, and experimental measurement of a pendulum ball impact-excited PEH. The key characteristic of this PEH is the use of a pendulum configuration to convert low-frequency ambient vibration to a highfrequency collision between the pendulum ball and piezoelectric cantilevers. As such, the power generation performance at low frequency is considerably improved. Compared with the previous research, the performance of the single pendulum ball structure has been improved by about six times. Moreover, the bi-pendulum ball structure can interact with two piezoelectric cantilever beams in one collision, thereby exhibiting a higher output performance across a lowoptimized load resistance. Through experimental results, the bi-pendulum ball impact-excited PEH achieves almost a fourfold increase in output power $( 4 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { W } )$ and one-third reduction in optimized load resistance $( 4 7 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega )$ at $2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ vibration frequency. The maximum output power density of the pendulum ball structure is $1 4 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { W } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 } ~ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 2 }$ . Furthermore, the bipendulum ball impact-excited PEH is suitable for a variety of vibrations, both linear and rotational. Table 3.
